I almost went down in front of the whole congregation on Easter Sunday.

Right there in the center aisle. Third pew from the front. Communion tray in my hands.

I remember the moment my knees started to buckle. The way the sanctuary tilted just a little to the left, like somebody had bumped the whole building. The stained glass window behind the pulpit went from a bright red cross to a smear of pink. I heard Pastor Whitfield say something about the blood of the lamb but his voice sounded like it was coming from under water.

My muscles were tight because something else was making them tight — and no one in twelve years of physical therapy, massage, or ergonomic consultation ever screened me for what was actually firing them.
For twelve years, I "managed" a condition I didn't actually have.

Twelve years of weekly deep-tissue massage. Same therapist. Rachel. She has known the exact knot in my right trap by name for over a decade. She calls it "the boulder." She has spent probably 500 hours of her life

My granddaughter announced her engagement on a Sunday and I told her yes before she finished asking.

She wanted me to make the cake.

I said yes and I smiled and I hugged her and I told her Grandma wouldn't miss it for the world.

Then I drove home and sat in my car in the driveway for 40 minutes crying so hard my glasses fogged up and I had to take them off and set them on the dashboard.

Because I haven't touched a piping bag in two and a half years.

I was diagnosed with fibromyalgia at 60. I'm 67 now. Turns out I never had fibromyalgia at all.

For seven years, I "managed" a condition I didn't actually have.

They started me on a nerve-pain medication that took the edge off for a few hours, then dropped me right back where I began. When that stopped helping, they added an antidepressant and told me it would "work on the pain." It didn't.
